_what_this_is: Every asymmetric key this system trusts, or has trusted, with its key_id RE-DERIVED FROM ITS OWN PUBLIC KEY BYTES and never taken from a label. It exists because two distinct Ed25519 keys both carried the comment 'claude-code@ct211', from a build host that no longer exists, and telling them apart took a fingerprint comparison against a backup file. A label is a claim; a key_id is a fact about the bytes. Both are recorded here, and where they disagree the bytes win.
_key_id_derivation: key_id = SHA-256(raw public key)[0:16], lowercase hex ('sha256-raw-16'). Identical to virp_fed_compute_key_id() in src/virp_federation.c, to include/virp_chainsign.h, and to the scheme the Docket verifier and the witness submitter registry already use. public_key_hex is the RAW 32-byte Ed25519 public key — the exact bytes the hash is taken over — so scripts/check-key-registry.sh can re-derive every id in this file from this file alone. Where a key is normally seen in another encoding (approvers.json uses base64 DER SPKI, SSH uses the ssh-ed25519 wire blob, minisign uses its own 2+8+32 blob), the raw bytes here are the last 32 bytes of that structure and the entry says so.
_append_only: ENTRIES ARE NEVER REMOVED AND NEVER REWRITTEN. A receipt, an approval or a chain head signed under a key must stay verifiable after that key is retired, and a verifier that cannot find the key it needs reports UNVERIFIABLE rather than 'not signed by anyone'. Retiring a key is a status change and a note, not a deletion. A key whose host is decommissioned keeps its entry with the real status, because 'this key was trusted on a machine that no longer exists' is exactly the fact that was expensive to reconstruct the last time. Correcting a mistake means adding a note, not editing history: the only field that legitimately changes after an entry is written is `status`, plus an appended note explaining the change.

_roles.chain-signing: Ed25519 signature over a chain head. The chain head's head_sig_key_id names this key.
_roles.witness-submitter: the identity a node presents when submitting heads to the witness. On the home node this is the SAME key as its chain-signing key, by design — the witness leaf's key_id then matches the head's head_sig_key_id and a reader can bind them without a second registry lookup.
_roles.witness: the witness log's own key, signing STHs.
_roles.approver: an operator identity in a node's approvers.json, authorising gate-blocked proposals.
_roles.seal: signs a periodic seal over the chain (tools/seal). Held as a minisign key.
_roles.producer: an evidence producer outside the daemon — camera segments, detection records — signing bodies the chain then commits to.
_roles.deploy: an SSH key used to reach or deploy to a node. Not a VIRP protocol key; recorded here because the ct211 incident was an SSH-key incident and a registry that omits them would not have caught it.

_roles_is_an_array: Deviation, stated rather than hidden: `roles` is a list, not a single string. c1104805 both signs the home node's chain heads and is the identity it submits them under. Splitting that into two entries would put the same key_id in the file twice, and key_id is this registry's primary key — the one thing that must be unique. One key with two jobs is one entry.
_public_half_seen_at: Where the PUBLIC half is enrolled or present, host:path. Not in the original field list, added because without it the registry cannot answer the question that motivated it. 'Where is this key trusted?' is what took a fingerprint sweep across two hosts and four containerlab directories to answer for the ct211 keys; a file that records the key but not its reach would have to be swept again.
_what_is_deliberately_absent: SYMMETRIC keys, and only those. /etc/virp/keys/onode.key (the O-Key, HMAC over v1 observations) and /etc/virp/keys/chain.key (K_chain, HMAC over chain entries) have NO public half. Their key_id under the same scheme is SHA-256 of the SECRET bytes, so deriving one means reading the secret, and a registry entry for it would be a hash of a live secret sitting in git. They are named here so their absence reads as a decision rather than an oversight. NOTHING ELSE IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: an earlier version of this file also excluded key 4727a5b94680ba53812ec49a42fe77ad as 'trusted nowhere', which was wrong — it had signed 32 chain records. See its entry. A key is in scope if it is pinned anywhere OR has signed anything.
_provenance: Populated 2026-09-03 by reading the public halves on virp-lab (10.0.10.211), virp-onode-home (10.0.0.13), the Spark (10.0.0.15) and this laptop, read-only. Every key_id below was derived from the bytes read, not copied from any declaration. valid_from is the mtime of the public-key file on the host that holds it, in UTC — it is the earliest hard evidence available, NOT a certificate validity date, and for keys copied between hosts it is the earliest mtime seen. Where a derived id confirmed an independently recorded one, the entry says so.

ADDENDUM 2026-09-03, appended not rewritten, per _append_only: the blast radius is now measured. 2537 camera_segment/1 records on the home node's chain (2026-08-24 to 08-26) are signed under this key. Retiring it and issuing per-machine keys would fix what future records bind and would change NOTHING about those 2537 — a signature cannot be retroactively narrowed. So the two options are not alternatives: the claim about the existing records has to change whatever is done about the key. What these 2537 records prove is that a body was signed by the holder of 008353cf and has not been altered since. They do not identify WHICH host produced it, and no future action can make them.

CORRECTS AN ERROR IN THIS FILE'S OWN FIRST VERSION, written earlier the same day. That version named this key in _what_is_deliberately_absent and declined to register it, on the stated grounds that it was 'trusted nowhere' and therefore not the ct211 case. That was wrong. It is not PINNED anywhere — but it has SIGNED 32 camera_segment records on the home node's chain (9 of schema /1, 23 of /2, 2026-08-29 to 08-31), which are the most RECENT camera evidence that node holds. Its public half is absent from /var/lib/virp/camera/, so those 32 records cannot be verified on the node that stores them: signed evidence with no reachable trust root, which reads as UNVERIFIABLE rather than as anything false. Copying its producer.pub to the node closes it and is named as an open item in SESSION-SUMMARY-COVERAGE-TRUST.md. The lesson is the one the registry was built to teach and then briefly failed to apply to itself: 'trusted nowhere' was inferred from where the key was ENROLLED, and the chain is the other place to look. Completeness is checked by sweeping what has SIGNED, not only what is pinned.
